01 / UNDERSTAND

Understanding fire.
Beyond gravity.

The chemistry of combustion remains the same. The movement of heat, fuel and oxygen changes.

Why does the flame change shape?

ILLUSTRATIVE COMPARISON

On Earth, buoyancy drives hot gases upwards and draws fresh air into a flame. This produces the familiar teardrop shape. In microgravity, this upward flow is greatly reduced. In a still atmosphere, a small diffusion flame can become roughly spherical as oxygen reaches it from all directions.

Illustrative flame shapes and transport. In microgravity, ventilation can still reshape a flame.

PHYSICS OF COMBUSTION

How heating can lead to fire.

Temperature and reaction rateRadical reactionsThermal decompositionDroplet combustionExtinction and oxygen limits

Arrhenius equation

The Arrhenius equation describes how temperature influences the rate constant of a chemical reaction:

k=Ae−EaRT
k
Reaction rate constant.
A
Pre-exponential factor; its units match those of k.
Ea
Activation energy, in J mol−1.
R
Gas constant, approximately 8.314 J mol−1 K−1.
T
Absolute temperature, in kelvin (K).

The rate constant describes one part of the reaction kinetics. It is not, by itself, a prediction of flame temperature or ignition.

Radicals and chain branching

Free radicals are atoms or molecules containing an unpaired electron. They can react to create more radicals, a process called chain branching. The balance between radical production and radical removal influences whether combustion can sustain itself.

A fire detection system could potentially identify chemical intermediates associated with oxidation, rather than relying exclusively on visible light or smoke.

Pyrolysis: thermal decomposition before a flame

When solid materials like wood, paper, plastics or textiles are exposed to high heat, thermal energy can break down their chemical bonds, releasing gases and organic vapours from the surface. Some of these products are flammable. Pyrolysis does not require oxygen, so a material can begin producing combustible gases before it catches fire.

If an electrical fault or another heat source causes a material to overheat, thermal decomposition can release gases before a developed flame exists. A detection system could investigate unusual volatile organic compounds (VOCs) associated with material degradation. However, normal spacecraft activities can also release VOCs, so the system would need to recognise abnormal combinations rather than treat every VOC measurement as evidence of fire.

Thermal decomposition is not the same for every material.

Different polymers have different chemical structures and therefore produce different decomposition products. This should be taken into account when designing the system.

Thermal runaway

Thermal runaway occurs when a process generates heat faster than the system can remove it, causing temperature to rise and potentially accelerate further heat generation, creating a positive feedback loop.

Rate of heat accumulation=Rate of heat generation−Rate of heat loss

A fire detection system could monitor not just temperature, but the rate at which temperature is changing.

A conceptual sequence. Processes can overlap; pyrolysis is a form of thermal decomposition, not a separate process that always follows it.
StageProcessDescription
1HeatingMaterial absorbs thermal energy.
2Thermal decompositionChemical structures begin breaking down.
3PyrolysisVolatile decomposition products are released.
4OxidationFuel products react with oxygen.
5Radical chain reactionsReactive intermediates participate in combustion.
6IgnitionSustained combustion develops.

How a liquid droplet keeps burning

  1. Heat from the flame reaches the liquid.
  2. The liquid evaporates, releasing fuel vapour.
  3. Fuel vapour moves outwards from the droplet.
  4. Oxygen moves towards the flame from the surrounding atmosphere.
  5. The fuel and oxygen react in a region surrounding the droplet.

How to read the diagram

Read from the droplet surface towards the surrounding atmosphere. Fuel vapour moves outward and oxygen moves inward, meeting at the idealised flame sheet. The curves illustrate temperature and composition; they are not measured FLEX results.

T means temperature and Y means mass fraction. The diagram draws rs from the centre to the droplet surface, so it is a radius; the original legend’s “droplet diameter” label is incorrect. rF is the radial position of the flame sheet.

This thin-flame model simplifies the reaction zone. It does not describe every flame shape or capture all the chemistry of cool flames.

Flames surviving at lower oxygen levels

FLEX measured limiting oxygen indices of approximately 12% for methanol and 15% for n-heptane in oxygen–nitrogen atmospheres. These are oxygen mole fractions for the reported droplet experiments, not universal material limits or safe cabin settings.

Published results: Dietrich et al. (2014), Droplet Combustion Experiments Aboard the International Space Station, abstract, pp. 65–66. Read the paper ↗

Two extinction mechanisms

Diffusive extinction

The reacting gases have insufficient residence time for the flame to sustain itself. This can occur as the flame shrinks towards the droplet. It is not simply the disappearance of oxygen, and diffusion does not stop in microgravity.

Radiative extinction

A flame emits thermal radiation, transferring energy away from the reaction zone. When heat losses are too large for the reactions to sustain the flame temperature, the hot flame extinguishes.

Nayagam et al. (2013): methanol droplet extinction, section 3.3.

How the two limits meet

As oxygen concentration decreased, the droplet diameter associated with diffusive extinction increased, while the diameter associated with radiative extinction decreased. Their meeting point identified the limiting oxygen index for quasi-steady combustion.

Reduced buoyancy changes the transport of heat, fuel and oxygen. Diffusion becomes more important in still microgravity, while fuel chemistry and heat losses continue to matter. Low oxygen concentration or a weak-looking flame alone does not establish a low fire risk.

Small flames in narrow spaces.

FLAMELETS

Flamelets are small, three-dimensional flames that form when a broad flame front becomes too weak to remain connected. Instead of extinguishing everywhere at once, the front can break into individual flames separated by gaps of non-burning material. This behaviour occurs under “near-limit” conditions: the flame is close to the conditions at which it can no longer sustain combustion.

Nearby wall · heat can be lost here
Fuel surface · unburned gaps separate the flamelets

A connected flame front spreads along the fuel surface. Select the near-limit example to see the front separated into smaller flames.

Illustrative comparison of a continuous flame front and separate flamelets.

Why does a flame front break apart?

A sustained flame needs both a supply of reactants and enough heat to keep its chemical reactions going. If oxygen becomes limited or heat is removed too quickly, parts of the flame front may no longer sustain combustion. Under some conditions, smaller regions continue burning while the spaces between them stop. These surviving regions are flamelets.

01 / CONFINEMENT

Heat escapes into nearby walls.

In a narrow gap, the flame is close to surrounding surfaces. Heat can transfer into these surfaces rather than remaining in the reacting gases. This heat loss weakens the flame and can bring it close to extinction.

02 / OXYGEN SUPPLY

Less oxygen can weaken the reaction.

Reducing oxygen concentration limits the oxidiser available for combustion. A broad flame front may become unstable or break into smaller flames before burning stops completely. The outcome depends on the fuel, heat losses and flow conditions together.

03 / AIRFLOW

Flow supplies oxygen and removes heat.

Incoming air can bring fresh oxygen to the flame, but it can also cool the reacting gases and remove combustion products. Very weak flow may not supply enough oxygen. Changing the flow can produce a connected front, separate flamelets or extinction; there is no single airflow rule that applies to every configuration.

How does the Narrow Channel Apparatus help?

The Narrow Channel Apparatus (NCA) places the burning material within a small gap. Researchers can vary oxygen concentration, incoming flow velocity and heat loss to nearby surfaces to investigate how a flame changes near its extinction limit.

The narrow channel also restricts buoyancy-driven flow. This allows some aspects of low-gravity flame spread to be investigated in a laboratory on Earth. It does not remove gravity: comparisons with drop-tower experiments help assess how well the apparatus represents the behaviour being studied.

Can a flame spread against the airflow?

Yes. Creeping flames can spread in the opposite direction to the incoming gas flow. Fresh oxygen reaches the leading edge of the flame while the flow carries combustion products away. The same flow also has a cooling effect. The direction in which a flame spreads is therefore not necessarily the direction in which smoke travels.

WHY SMALL FLAMES MATTER

A weak flame can still spread through a concealed space.

Flamelets can burn within narrow gaps behind panels or around insulation, where the source is difficult to see. Smoke may be detected without revealing the location of the burning material. If the flame reaches a region with a different oxygen supply, airflow or geometry, the conditions supporting its growth can change.

This is why a small or weak-looking flame should not be confused with a fire that has stopped. Detecting smoke, locating the source and understanding the surrounding flow are separate parts of assessing the situation.

Flamelet research references

  • ScienceDirect — flamelet research paper ↗
  • Fire in Microgravity — American Scientist ↗

Why this matters for detection.

Small flames may be concealed behind panels or within narrow gaps. Smoke can reach a detector before the source is easy to locate. Electrical faults, overheating equipment and flammable materials remain relevant hazards in microgravity.

01 / FLEX · TWO COMBUSTION REGIMES

Understanding
cool flames.

FLEX revealed that, under certain conditions, a cool flame can continue burning after the visible hot flame has been extinguished. The sequence below explains how this transition occurs.

How droplet combustion works

A liquid fuel droplet releases vapour, which mixes and reacts with oxygen in the surrounding air. The flame forms around the droplet, where these gases meet. In microgravity, the absence of buoyant rise allows a roughly spherical flame to form. The diagrams compare continued hot burning with the transition to cool burning observed under certain conditions in FLEX.

Cool flame
A lower-temperature flame that can continue burning after the visible hot flame is extinguished under certain conditions.
Extinction
The end of a sustained flame. Hot-flame extinction does not always mean that all combustion has stopped.
Fuel vapour
Fuel in its gaseous form, released from the liquid droplet. It reacts with oxygen around the droplet.

HOW A HOT FLAME STARTS

Starting a hot flame.

Fuel vapour and oxygen need suitable conditions and an ignition source, such as a heated igniter. In a droplet experiment, the fuel vaporises and burns around the liquid. Once established, heat from combustion can sustain the reaction. This is the route shown in both panels.

HOW THIS COOL FLAME STARTS

Starting a cool flame.

In the FLEX pathway, heat loss extinguishes the hot flame. Under certain fuel and atmosphere conditions, lower-temperature oxidation continues around the droplet. This does not happen after every fire goes out. Cool flames can also arise during heating or compression of suitable fuel–air mixtures; that is a different initiation route.

NASA: the FLEX discovery ↗
COOL DOES NOT MEAN SAFE

Temperature and combustion products.

Cool flames can burn at temperatures around 400 °C, although the temperature depends on the fuel and surrounding conditions. Low-temperature chemistry can produce carbon monoxide and formaldehyde. Hot flames can also produce incomplete-combustion products: neither colour nor visibility establishes safe air.

NASA: cool-flame chemistry ↗
02 / ACME · FLAME DESIGN

Reducing
soot production.

Soot forms and grows in fuel-rich regions; some can oxidise before leaving the flame. Change these two processes separately to see why formation and emission are different.

How soot forms and leaves a flame

Soot consists of carbon-rich particles formed during incomplete combustion. Some of these particles are consumed by further chemical reactions before they leave the flame. This process is called oxidation. The diagrams distinguish soot formation from soot emission: the amount produced inside a flame is not necessarily the amount released into the exhaust.

Soot
Carbon-rich solid particles produced during incomplete combustion.
Oxidation
Chemical reactions that consume soot before it leaves the flame.
Emission
The release of surviving soot particles into the exhaust.

1. Formation

In fuel-rich regions, where fuel is abundant relative to oxygen, incomplete combustion can produce carbon-rich particles. These particles may grow and join together. Peach dots represent soot forming within the flame.

2. Oxidation

Soot reacts with oxygen and other reactive species, consuming some of the solid particles. The blue dots fade to represent this removal. The amount consumed depends on the conditions and time available for reaction.

→

3. Emission

Particles that survive oxidation can leave the flame with the exhaust. Grey dots crossing the dashed line represent these emissions. Reducing formation and increasing oxidation are different ways to reduce the soot that escapes.

WHAT NASA STUDIED

Designing the flame, not just filtering the exhaust.

One ACME investigation, called Flame Design, studied how different flame conditions affect soot production in spherical gaseous-fuel flames. The research aims to inform combustion systems with lower unwanted soot. Explore the balance between soot formation and oxidation in the demonstration.
